At Fernways School, inclusivity shines brightly as we embrace each child and young person's unique journey, ensuring no one is left behind. Our aim is to cultivate independent or interdependent, resilient, confident, and motivated young people.
Central to this vision is the belief that strong, trusting relationships between staff and students form the foundation for meaningful learning and personal growth. We understand that when students feel valued, understood, and supported, they are more engaged, motivated, and ready to overcome challenges.
My vision for Fernways School is one that establishes a flourishing learning community defined by personalised learning experiences, collaborative learning, and academic rigour contextualised within real-world experiences. Equally important is our commitment to creating an environment highly attentive to the social, emotional, and mental health needs of our students. We care deeply about how our students feel and strive to ensure they are happy and healthy, both inside and outside of school.
At Fernways, we nurture each student by providing the social, emotional, and communicative support they need to navigate the wider world as we prepare them for their next steps in life. Our goal is to equip them with the skills to tackle whatever comes their way with confidence and resilience.
I am truly passionate about my role and the opportunity to lead such a dedicated team in supporting our students on this exciting path to growth and success. I warmly welcome you to be part of the Fernways community.
Nikeisha Webb-Hardy
What We Offer
Our vision is to deliver a creative curriculum that is personalised for every student. We recognise that each child is unique, and so our curriculum is carefully adapted to reflect individual interests, strengths, and learning needs. This approach ensures that all students can make meaningful progress academically and personally, developing into well-rounded young people ready for the next stages of their lives.
At Fernways, we understand that academic progress is just one part of a child’s development. Our holistic approach supports emotional, social, and physical well-being, recognising the complex needs many of our students face.
We understand that therapy plays a vital role in unlocking potential. That’s why we provide a carefully mapped, integrated therapy provision tailored to each student’s individual needs. From universal to specialised therapies, our team tracks progress closely and shares outcomes with parents and staff, ensuring every child receives the support they need to thrive academically, socially, and emotionally.
At Fernways School, we are committed to equipping our students with the essential life skills and vocational experiences they need to thrive beyond school. Our personalised curriculum includes practical learning opportunities that foster independence, confidence, and real-world readiness. Through tailored work experience placements, community projects, and skill-building activities, we help students develop the competencies necessary for adulthood, empowering them to pursue meaningful careers and lead fulfilling lives. Our dedicated team works closely with students, families, and local employers to create pathways that celebrate each student’s strengths and aspirations.
We are passionate about raising career and educational aspirations, equipping students with the skills and confidence they need for life beyond school.
Safeguarding is at the heart of everything we do
As part of the Kedleston Group, our school follows robust safeguarding standards to keep every child safe, supported and protected.
Safeguarding at the Kedleston Group
Part of the Kedleston Group
We’re proud to be part of the Kedleston Group family of schools, all committed to providing safe, nurturing and ambitious education for neurodivergent learners.
About the Kedleston Group
Accreditations and memberships

About Us
Kedleston Group opened the doors to its first school in 2006 and now operates 20 specialist schools and children’s homes in the UK. Each year we support over 700 children from over 80 Local Authorities.
Our Journey
Today, we have over 700 employees, whom have considerable industry expertise and are at the forefront of innovative teaching and care support.
Our frontline education and care staff are supported by highly skilled clinical teams and have the backing of Governance, Recruitment, HR, Quality and other teams, providing a robust support framework for schools and children’s homes, allowing them to concentrate on the children.
“I have been here 6 years and have progressed into a more senior role, I have been supported by Kedleston Group as a whole. They promote positive health and wellbeing and are very supportive in all aspects of my life. The benefits are great.”
Our Culture & Ambition
Our mission is to develop confident and capable children by meeting their educational, health and social care needs in nurturing school and home provisions.
We are ambitious for the children we support; we work in partnership alongside their families and carers and other stakeholders to achieve outcomes which make a difference. Preparing each child with the skills and confidence to continue their journey into further education and beyond.
Our Values
We put quality at the heart of everything we do and have a culture of ‘high expectations’ for all our children.
What we do is important, and we work hard to get the best results for all our children.
Our children have rights, opinions and goals and we work with them as individuals.
Safeguarding/Child Protection is one of our key priorities. We strive to ensure all our children are kept safe.
We work in partnership with all stakeholders.
We invest in our people & premises.
We are honest, fair and ethical in everything we do.
We accept responsibility for our actions.
“I enjoy seeing the progress in the children. I have worked my way up from a Care Worker position here, and I absolutely love my job. The staff team are fantastic and there is a real community feel.”

SEND glossary
SEND - Special Educational Needs and/or Disabilities
SEN - Special Educational Needs
SENCO/SENDCO - Special Educational Needs Coordinator/Special Educational Needs and/or Disabilities Coordinator
EHCP – Education, Health and Care Plan
IEP – Individual Education Plan
Annual Review – Yearly review of a child’s EHCP
Local Offer – Directory of SEND services provided by the local authority
Provision Map – Overview of support provided to pupils with SEND
ASC / ASD – Autism Spectrum Condition / Disorder
ADHD – Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
ADD – Attention Deficit Disorder (without hyperactivity)
SpLD – Specific Learning Difficulties (e.g., dyslexia, dyspraxia)
MLD – Moderate Learning Difficulty
SLD – Severe Learning Difficulty
PMLD – Profound and Multiple Learning Difficulties
SEMH – Social, Emotional and Mental Health Needs
SLCN – Speech, Language and Communication Needs
VI – Visual Impairment
HI – Hearing Impairment
SI – Sensory Integration difficulties
Tourette’s Syndrome – Neurological condition involving tics
Dyslexia – A set of processing difficulties that affect the acquisition of reading and spelling. (Read more - Delphi definition - British Dyslexia Association)
Dyspraxia – A common, lifelong neurological condition affecting physical coordination, motor planning, and organisation (Read more - NHS)
Dyscalculia – Often used to describe someone who unexpectedly struggles to understand and achieve in Maths (Read more - British Dyslexia Association)
Special School – A school specifically for children with complex SEND
Mainstream School – General education school
Alternative Provision (AP) – Education outside traditional education settings
Independent Specialist School – Non-maintained school offering specialist SEND support
Panel – Multi-agency group reviewing school placements and EHCPs
Placement Consultation – Process of matching a child with a suitable school
Named School – School listed in Section I of the EHCP
Tribunal – Legal appeal process for EHCP decisions
Consultation/Referral - The process of a Local Authority sending a child's Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP), along with any supporting documents, to a school for consideration for a place
EP – Educational Psychologist
CAMHS – Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services
SaLT – Speech and Language Therapist
OT – Occupational Therapist
Physio – Physiotherapist
QTVI – Qualified Teacher of the Visually Impaired
QTMSI – Qualified Teacher of the Multi-Sensory Impaired
TAC – Team Around the Child
Early Help – Support for families before statutory interventio
CLA / LAC – Child Looked After / Looked After Child
UASC – Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Child
MASH – Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub
CP Plan – Child Protection Plan
DSL – Designated Safeguarding Lead
Reasonable Adjustments – Legal requirement to remove barriers for disabled pupils
Transition Plan – Support for moving between educational stages and/or settings
Person-Centred Planning – Approach focused on the child’s voice and aspirations
Outreach Support – Specialist advice provided to mainstream settings
EHCP Outcomes – Goals set in the EHCP to measure progress
Provision Panel – Local authority group deciding on specialist placement

Working together
We understand that every child experiences the world in their own unique way. That’s why our approach is always personalised, inclusive, and focused on unlocking potential. Through tailored education and care, we help neurodivergent learners grow into the confident, capable individuals they are meant to be.
Our admissions team are experts in matching each child’s needs to our schools, they consider a huge range of factors to give every child the best possible chance to thrive in education. We will only accept pupils whom we feel our schools can meet their needs.

Getting started

Welcome
At Kedleston Group, our shared purpose is to create bright futures for children with special educational needs and disabilities. We create safe, nurturing and supportive environments where every young person can flourish.
Our team of over 700 professionals is dedicated, compassionate and unwavering in its commitment to supporting children.
We recognise and celebrate the contribution of all colleagues and we invest in their development so that they can learn, grow and advance their careers. If you are driven by a desire to make a lasting difference in the lives of children and young people, we would love to hear from you! Learn more about us and explore our latest opportunities below.
Who Are We?
Kedleston Group is a family-owned group of independent specialist schools and children’s homes operating across the UK. Each year we support over 700 children from over 80 different Local Authorities through our specialist schools and children’s homes.
What We Do
We specialise in providing high-quality education and care for children aged 7-19 with a range of needs, including autistic spectrum condition, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or social emotional and mental health needs.
Specialist Schools: Our 14 specialist day schools deliver personalised programmes of education and therapeutic interventions. Enabling children to learn skills for life and achieve relevant qualifications and awards.
Children’s Homes: Our children’s homes provide children with a safe and nurturing environment offering warm round-the-clock care and support where they can thrive and reach their potential.
Each of our provisions are tailored to meet the young person’s individual needs to provide the best opportunities to thrive and flourish.
Our schools follow the National Curriculum and have a strong educational focus. For many of our young people their previous experience in education has been a negative one, so we aim to re-ignite a passion for learning.
Our homes work to provide children with fantastic care which includes memorable experiences and results in positive outcomes for children and young people. We want the children we care for to have fun and be safe whilst they are with us and to feel treasured for who they are.
“We get to be involved in a lot of fun activities, and it feels like a real community. We work with lots of interesting people, and I enjoy the social aspects. It’s a lovely place to work. I have good relationships with the children.”

Welcome
At Kedleston Group, our shared purpose is to create bright futures for children with special educational needs and disabilities. We create safe, nurturing and supportive environments where every young person can flourish.
Our team of over 700 professionals is dedicated, compassionate and unwavering in its commitment to supporting children.
We recognise and celebrate the contribution of all colleagues and we invest in their development so that they can learn, grow and advance their careers. Who Are We?
Kedleston Group is a family-owned group of independent specialist schools and children’s homes operating across the UK. Each year we support over 700 children from over 80 different Local Authorities through our specialist schools and children’s homes.
What We Do
We specialise in providing high-quality education and care for children aged 7-19 with a range of needs, including autistic spectrum condition, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or social emotional and mental health needs.
Specialist Schools: Our 14 specialist day schools deliver personalised programmes of education and therapeutic interventions. Enabling children to learn skills for life and achieve relevant qualifications and awards.
Children’s Homes: Our children’s homes provide children with a safe and nurturing environment offering warm round-the-clock care and support where they can thrive and reach their potential.
Each of our provisions are tailored to meet the young person’s individual needs to provide the best opportunities to thrive and flourish.
Our schools follow the National Curriculum and have a strong educational focus. For many of our young people their previous experience in education has been a negative one, so we aim to re-ignite a passion for learning.
Our homes work to provide children with fantastic care which includes memorable experiences and results in positive outcomes for children and young people. We want the children we care for to have fun and be safe whilst they are with us and to feel treasured for who they are.

Understanding the process
At Kedleston Group, we work in close partnership with families and Local Authorities to ensure our schools are the right fit for each learner. Our admissions process is designed to be clear, compassionate, and centred around the needs of the child.
All of our schools follow the Kedleston Group admissions process.
*Please note, whilst we accept parental enquiries, we cannot accept referrals directly from parents.
1. Initial referral
The first step is for the Local Authority to make a formal consultation to our Admissions Team. This will include the child or young person’s Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) and any relevant supporting documentation. Local Authorities will usually consult with several settings.
2. Paperwork review
Our Admissions Team will then carry out an initial assessment by reviewing the referral paperwork to understand the child’s needs and determine whether we may be able to meet them.
3. Assessment visit
If appropriate, we’ll invite the child and their family to attend an assessment visit to school. This includes a tour of the setting and an opportunity to meet the Headteacher and key staff. It’s a chance for families to ask questions and for us to better understand your child's needs.
4. Placement offer
Following the assessment visit, and if we believe we can meet your child’s needs, we will send an offer letter to the Local Authority with a proposed start date.
5. Transition planning
Once the offer is agreed, we’ll work closely with you, the child’s current setting, and the Local Authority to plan a smooth and supportive transition.
Consultation progress is always communicated with your child’s Local Authority.

Therapeutic approach
Our therapeutic practice is grounded in a tiered provision model that places therapeutic, informed intervention at the centre of every student’s experience. Rather than viewing therapy as an add on, this approach weaves therapeutic thinking, strategies and environments into the daily life of the school. It ensures that every student benefits from a foundation of emotional understanding and support, while also having access to more targeted or specialist intervention when needed.
How the tiered model works
A flexible, needs‑Led system
A key strength of this model is its fluidity. Pupils are not fixed within a tier; instead, they move between levels of provision depending on their current needs, circumstances and progress. This dynamic approach ensures that support is always responsive, timely and appropriate.
Why this matters
By embedding therapeutic thinking into the fabric of the school and offering a flexible continuum of support, we create an environment where pupils feel understood, safe, and empowered. This foundation enables them to develop the emotional resilience and confidence they need to flourish both academically and personally.
What this look like in school
Each Kedleston Group school is supported by an on‑site therapy team that is bespoke to its individual community. The composition of this team, including the range of therapeutic disciplines, interventions and facilities available, is shaped by the needs of the school’s cohort and therefore varies from school to school. This flexible approach ensures that therapy provision is relevant, responsive and fully aligned with the specific needs of the pupils each school serves.
Occupational Therapy in Kedleston Group schools supports children to develop the practical, emotional, sensory and cognitive skills they need to participate confidently in learning and everyday life. Our Occupational Therapists begin with a detailed assessment of each pupil’s strengths, challenges and sensory processing profile. This helps them understand how the child experiences the world and what support will help them feel safe, regulated and ready to learn.
Intervention plans are personalised and integrated naturally into the school day. Children may work on developing fine and gross motor skills, improving handwriting fluency, building core strength, learning functional routines or managing sensory overwhelm. Sessions can be delivered individually, in small groups or within the classroom environment. Therapists also design sensory diets, sensory circuits, environmental adaptations and movement-based routines that help pupils stay calm, focused and comfortable throughout the day.
Collaboration is a core part of the service. OTs work closely with teachers, pastoral staff and families so that strategies are consistent across home and school. This joined-up approach ensures progress is meaningful and long-lasting. Small steps are celebrated, and pupils grow in confidence as they develop the skills that support independence, engagement and wellbeing.Optional apprentice line
Our OT team may also be supported by a trained Occupational Therapy Apprentice who works under the supervision of a qualified therapist to deliver elements of the programme and provide day-to-day support for pupils.
Speech and Language Therapy within Kedleston Group schools focuses on helping every learner develop communication skills that are useful, meaningful and empowering in everyday life. Therapists begin by looking at how a learner understands language, how they express themselves, how they interact with others, their speech clarity, and how they use non-verbal communication such as gestures or facial expressions.This helps us build a clear picture of each learner’s individual communication strengths and needs.
Support is tailored to each learner. It may include one-to-one sessions, small group work, or support in the classroom. Activities are practical and engaging, and may focus on building vocabulary, developing sentences, improving speech sounds, supporting attention and listening, or developing social skills such as turn-taking and conversation. For neurodivergent learners, we use a respectful, neuroaffirming approach. This may include visual supports, simplified language, or alternative ways of communicating to help learners feel comfortable and confident.We place a strong focus on communication skills that learners can use in real life. This includes helping them to make choices, ask for help, share ideas, and express their feelings in a way that works for them. Speech and Language Therapists work closely with parents, teachers, and other professionals so that strategies can be used consistently at home and in school. This joined-up approach helps learners build communication skills that support learning, friendships, and overall wellbeing.
Psychotherapy in Kedleston Group schools provides a calm, supportive space where pupils can explore thoughts and feelings that may be difficult to express in everyday life. Sessions are designed around the child’s individual needs and can include talking, creative work, play-based exploration or reflective activities. The therapeutic relationship offers safety and containment, which allows pupils to develop emotional understanding and resilience.
Psychotherapists help children make sense of their internal world and understand why certain experiences may feel overwhelming. Themes may include confidence, identity, emotional regulation, anxiety, past experiences or relationships. Therapy progresses at the pace of the pupil and places the child’s well-being at the centre of every session.
Therapists work collaboratively with teaching teams and families, while maintaining appropriate therapeutic boundaries. This ensures adults have insight into the child’s emotional needs and can support them consistently across contexts. The overall aim is to help pupils feel more secure, confident and capable of engaging positively with learning and daily life.
Clinical Psychology within Kedleston Group schools provides specialist assessment, therapeutic intervention and consultation for pupils with complex emotional, behavioural or developmental needs. Clinical Psychologists draw on advanced training in mental health, neurodiversity and trauma to understand each child’s unique presentation.
The service begins with thorough assessments that explore emotional wellbeing, psychological functioning and contributing factors in the child’s wider environment. Findings are brought together through psychological formulation, which helps identify what the child needs and how best to support them.
Intervention may include cognitive behavioural strategies, trauma-informed work, emotional regulation techniques, creative therapeutic approaches or structured problem-solving. Clinical Psychologists also provide significant indirect support. This includes consultation, reflective practice, staff training and guidance on supporting complex behaviour. Their expertise strengthens the capacity of the whole school and supports a psychologically safe and nurturing environment.
Kedleston Group schools work with experienced Educational Psychology professionals who offer specialist insight into how children learn and engage with their environment. They assess cognitive strengths, barriers to learning, memory, processing, attention and executive functioning. Their input helps shape personalised learning approaches that support pupils to access the curriculum more effectively.
They also provide consultation and reflective guidance to teaching staff. This helps teams understand the psychological factors that influence learning and behaviour. Recommendations may include adjustments to classroom structure, strategies that reduce cognitive load, techniques that support emotional regulation or approaches that help pupils engage more confidently.
The work of Educational Psychology professionals contributes to a learning environment that is thoughtful, inclusive and adapted to the needs of every individual.
Mentors in Kedleston Group schools provide consistent emotional and practical support that helps pupils feel understood and valued. Each mentor builds a trusting relationship with their pupils and offers a safe space for them to talk through challenges, develop coping strategies and set personal goals.
Mentoring sessions may explore friendships, organisation, feelings, motivation or problem-solving. Mentors help pupils develop resilience and confidence, and they are often a grounding presence during moments of stress or transition. Because they work closely with pupils on a daily basis, mentors can identify subtle changes in wellbeing and help coordinate support with the wider team.
This relational approach strengthens pupils’ sense of belonging and directly supports engagement in learning.
ELSA practitioners deliver structured emotional literacy support that helps pupils understand their emotions and develop tools to manage them effectively. Working under the guidance of Educational Psychologists, ELSAs support children with issues such as anxiety, self-esteem, friendships, loss, anger management and social skills.
Sessions use creative and practical activities to help pupils explore feelings in a gentle and accessible way. Elsa's work is time-limited but highly impactful. Strategies are shared with teachers and families so pupils can continue to benefit long after the programme ends.
ELSA practitioners contribute to a calm and supportive school environment where pupils feel equipped to handle challenges and express themselves confidently.
Drawing and Talking is a therapeutic approach that allows children to express feelings that may be difficult to articulate verbally. In weekly one-to-one sessions, pupils create drawings that become the starting point for gentle, reflective conversations with a trained practitioner. The aim is not to analyse the artwork but to help the child externalise worries and process emotions at a pace that feels safe.
This approach is particularly helpful for pupils who may have experienced distressing events or who find it easier to communicate through images rather than words. Drawing and Talking support emotional organisation, reduce anxiety and help children develop a sense of internal stability.
Practitioners maintain confidentiality while working closely with school teams to ensure children receive the support they need across all aspects of school life.
LEGO Therapy is a structured, collaborative intervention that supports social communication and teamwork. Pupils take on specific roles within a small group and must communicate clearly and cooperatively to build a LEGO model together. This structure helps pupils practise turn-taking, listening, problem-solving and perspective-taking in a fun and motivating setting. Facilitators guide the group carefully to ensure communication remains positive and inclusive. The approach builds confidence, encourages cooperative behaviour and supports pupils in developing communication skills that transfer naturally to real-life social situations.
Guidance counsellors provide emotional and pastoral support that helps pupils navigate school life and personal challenges. They offer a confidential space where pupils can express concerns, reflect on difficulties and explore possible solutions. Support may focus on wellbeing, peer relationships, self-esteem, motivation or planning for the future.
Counsellors collaborate with teachers, pastoral teams and families so that pupils receive consistent support. They play a key role in safeguarding, crisis response and early intervention. Their presence helps pupils feel heard, supported and understood throughout their school journey.
Play and Creative Arts Therapy uses creative expression to help children make sense of emotional experiences. Pupils may work with materials such as sand trays, paint, storytelling, music or movement. These non-verbal approaches allow children to explore feelings safely and at their own pace.
This therapy is particularly effective for pupils who struggle to express themselves verbally or who have experienced trauma, anxiety or emotional overwhelm. Sessions support self-regulation, emotional literacy, confidence and resilience. Therapists work closely with staff and families so that pupils experience consistent support while therapeutic boundaries remain protected.
Assistant Psychologists support the wider psychology service by carrying out structured assessments, helping with data collection, contributing to formulations and delivering low-intensity interventions under supervision. They may also run wellbeing groups, offer targeted one-to-one work and support evidence-based programmes.
Their role strengthens the capacity of the psychology team and ensures pupils receive timely and consistent support. They also help staff understand pupils’ needs through observations, feedback and resource development.
Therapy Assistants work under the supervision of qualified therapists and psychologists to deliver practical and therapeutic support across the school. They help implement intervention programmes, run small-group activities, prepare resources and support children in applying therapeutic strategies in daily routines.
They also act as a familiar and consistent adult who can help pupils practise regulation skills, build confidence and engage more comfortably in school life. Therapy Assistants contribute to the overall continuity and quality of therapeutic provision throughout the school day.

What is an EHCP?
EHCP stands for Education, Health and Care Plan. It is a legal document used in England for children and young people aged 0-25 who need more support than a school or college can normally provide. EHCPs were introduced in 2014, replacing Statements of Special Educational Needs.
What does an ECHP do?
What does an EHCP do?
Details the support they must legally receive
What's included in an EHCP?
An EHCP is structured into clearly defined sections, each with its own letter and purpose, to set out a child’s needs and the specific education, health and care provision required
Section A - the child's views and aspirations
Section B - their special educational needs
Section C - their health needs related to SEN
Section D - their social care needs related to SEN
Section E - sets out the long-term, measurable outcomes the plan is aiming to achieve
Section F - the exact educational provision required to meet section B
Section G - health care provision required
Section H - social care provision required
Section I - the named school or setting and type of setting
Section J - details of agreed personal budget
Section K - an appendix of all advice, information and reports gathered during the assessment process
What is the process for creating an EHCP?
How long does the EHCP process take?
The EHCP process is governed by the legal timescale, which is defined under the Children and Families Act 2014. The entire process should take no more than 20 weeks from the time the Local Authority receives a request to the issuing of the final EHCP.
Included in this time are 6 weeks for the Local Authority to decide whether to assess the child's needs and then upto an additional 14 weeks to complete the assessment, consult and then issue the final plan.

Safeguarding
All children deserve to feel safe, supported, and valued. Every successful education journey begins with effective safeguarding. When children feel protected and cared for, they can develop confidence, build trusting relationships, and fully engage in learning. For this reason, safeguarding sits at the very heart of everything we do across the Kedleston Group.
A robust, system‑led approach to safeguarding
Safeguarding across the Kedleston Group is underpinned by clear structures, defined responsibilities, and consistent processes that operate across all schools. This ensures that safeguarding practice is not reliant on any one individual, but is embedded securely within the organisation at every level.
Each school has a Designated Safeguarding Lead who holds day‑to‑day responsibility for safeguarding within their setting. This role is supported and overseen through a Group‑wide safeguarding framework that ensures consistency, compliance, and continuous improvement.
At Group level, overall strategic oversight of safeguarding is provided through the role of Group Safeguarding Lead. This role ensures that robust safeguarding arrangements are in place across all schools, that statutory and regulatory requirements are met, and that safeguarding remains central to daily practice, decision making, and organisational culture.
Assurance, oversight and continuous improvement
To maintain the highest standards of safeguarding practice, a comprehensive safeguarding audit is undertaken annually across all schools within the Group. This audit reviews safeguarding systems, procedures, training, reporting processes, and the safeguarding culture within each setting. Its purpose is both to assure compliance and to identify opportunities to strengthen practice and improve outcomes for children.
In addition to the annual audit, regular safeguarding committee meetings take place within each school. These meetings provide professional support and appropriate challenge to school‑based safeguarding leads. They enable safeguarding concerns to be reviewed, actions to be monitored, learning from cases to be reflected upon, and responses to be evaluated for effectiveness and timeliness. This approach also supports the sharing of best practice across the Kedleston Group.
Governance and accountability
Safeguarding is subject to strong governance and scrutiny through the Safeguarding Overview Committee, which operates as a dedicated subcommittee of the Kedleston Group Board of Directors. This ensures that safeguarding is monitored, challenged, and prioritised at the highest level of the organisation. The Safeguarding Overview Committee is made up of senior leaders and governance representatives, including a Non‑Executive Director as Chair, the Chief Executive Officer, the Chief Operating Officer, the Group Safeguarding Lead, and a Committee Secretary.
The Committee reviews safeguarding matters across the Group, including emerging risks, themes, trends, and areas for development. Where necessary, it issues recommendations or requirements to further strengthen safeguarding arrangements. The Committee meets monthly and provides regular updates to the Board, ensuring clear lines of accountability and oversight.
External scrutiny and inspection
Our schools are registered with the Department for Education and are subject to inspection by Ofsted. These inspections provide independent assurance that our schools meet required standards and provide safe, high‑quality learning environments for children and young people.
Ofsted inspection reports can be accessed on the individual page for each school or by visiting the Ofsted website.
Across the Kedleston Group, safeguarding is more than a policy or procedure. It is a shared responsibility and a deeply embedded commitment to ensuring that every child feels safe, respected, and supported so they can thrive both in education and in wider life.
Career opportunities
We’re looking for passionate, driven people who want to help shape brighter futures for neurodiverse children and young people. At Kedleston Group, you’ll find a supportive community, meaningful work, and opportunities to grow your career.

Curriculum & Approach
At Fernways School, our curriculum is thoughtfully designed to meet the academic, social, and emotional needs of every student, reflecting our commitment to building Confidence, fostering Creativity, and nurturing a strong sense of Community. We follow the National Curriculum while offering a diverse range of subjects and qualifications, including Entry Levels, GCSEs, vocational, and functional skills qualifications, all tailored to empower our students.
Our curriculum’s primary aim is to equip students with the skills, independence, and confidence they need to flourish beyond school. We prepare them to achieve their ambitions—whether that’s progressing to college, pursuing apprenticeships, or engaging in further training—by providing meaningful qualifications and enriching experiences.
Core subjects such as Maths, English, and Science form the foundation of our curriculum, ensuring each student gains essential knowledge and qualifications from Entry Level to GCSE. Alongside these, we embrace a broad curriculum that mirrors the National Curriculum while embedding opportunities to develop creativity and confidence.
We are proud to offer unique subjects like ‘Preparing for Adulthood’ and ‘Outdoor Learning.’ These areas cultivate vital qualities such as problem-solving, resilience, creativity, teamwork, and planning, while reinforcing our commitment to community by encouraging collaboration and mutual support. Our curriculum is designed to help students transfer knowledge across subjects and apply their skills confidently in real-life contexts beyond the classroom.
Creativity is a cornerstone of our curriculum, with a wide variety of practical and expressive subjects including Art, Performing Arts, Design Technology, and Cooking. These subjects provide students with productive outlets for self-expression and innovation.
We also prioritise holistic development by integrating clinical and health support through a comprehensive programme of PE, Sports, Outdoor Education, occupational therapy, as well as speech and language therapy. This is complemented by a robust PSHRE and SRE curriculum, which supports personal development and promotes physical, mental, and sexual health and wellbeing.
At Fernways, our curriculum is more than just academic learning; it is a vibrant community experience that inspires creativity and builds the confidence every student needs to lead their own learning journey and thrive in adulthood
At Fernways School, we follow the National Curriculum, carefully adapted to meet the unique needs of our learners. Our curriculum is designed not only to provide a broad and balanced education but also to ensure that every student achieves success in a way that is meaningful and appropriate to their individual abilities and aspirations.
Our learners leave Fernways with a range of qualifications, from Entry Level qualifications through to GCSEs, tailored to their personal learning journey. We are committed to ensuring that all learners achieve some form of qualification, providing them with the skills, knowledge, and confidence needed to take their next steps—whether that be further education, apprenticeships, or other training opportunities.
The curriculum at Fernways is structured to enable students to master foundational concepts and skills before progressing, helping to build their confidence and promote success. We recognise the importance of linking new learning to existing knowledge, carefully sequencing teaching to support the development of increasingly complex understanding across all subject areas.
Core subjects such as English, Maths, and Science form the foundation of our curriculum, ensuring that every student gains essential skills and qualifications in these key areas. Alongside these, we offer a wide range of subjects including vocational and functional skills qualifications, enabling learners to develop practical skills and explore their interests.
Our curriculum also places a strong emphasis on communication, literacy, and numeracy, with teaching approaches that explicitly support these areas. We are committed to helping students overcome common learning challenges by anticipating misconceptions and providing targeted support.
At Fernways, the curriculum is more than just academic achievement; it is about preparing students for life beyond school. Our offer includes opportunities for students to develop social, communication, and independence skills, ensuring they are ready to thrive in their communities and future pathways.
We are proud that every learner leaves Fernways equipped with qualifications that reflect their achievements and readiness for the next stage of their journey.
At Fernways, we recognise that every pupil’s journey is unique. Our role is to provide clear education pathways while also offering the flexibility to adapt learning to individual needs, interests and ambitions. The Fernways Approach
Our pathways and flexible programmes are not just about gaining qualifications; they are about preparing pupils for life. Whether moving on to college, an apprenticeship, or supported employment, every pupil leaves Fernways with a personalised record of achievement, the confidence to succeed, and the experience of having been supported as an individual.

Flexibility ensures that pupils who may have struggled in previous settings can re-engage with learning, build confidence and move forward at a pace that suits them.
At Fernways School, we recognise that Outdoor Learning and Physical Education are vital components of our curriculum, playing a key role in fostering Confidence, Creativity, and Community among our students. As a specialist provision catering for children and young people who are neurodiverse, we understand the unique benefits that these experiences bring to our learners’ development.
Outdoor Learning provides a stimulating environment where students can engage with the natural world in meaningful ways. It encourages curiosity and creativity as students explore, problem-solve, and make connections between their learning and real-world contexts. This hands-on approach supports our learners in building complex mental models and transferring knowledge beyond the classroom, which is essential for their academic and personal growth.
Physical Education at Fernways is designed not only to promote physical health but also to develop self-confidence and social skills. Through a variety of activities tailored to individual needs and abilities, students gain resilience, improve coordination, and experience success in a supportive setting. PE sessions foster teamwork and cooperation, helping to build a strong sense of community and belonging—key values at Fernways.
Both Outdoor Learning and Physical Education contribute significantly to our students’ emotional wellbeing. They offer opportunities for self-expression, reduce anxiety, and support positive attitudes towards learning and personal achievement. These experiences are carefully integrated with therapeutic support and personalised learning plans to ensure they meet the diverse needs of our students.
By embracing Outdoor Learning and Physical Education, Fernways nurtures confident, creative learners who are equipped to engage with their communities and thrive in all aspects of life.
At Fernways School, we deliver a comprehensive Preparing for Adulthood curriculum, inclusive of relationship education, which enables our children to become healthy, independent, and responsible members of society. The Education Act (2002) requires that schools provide children with a broad and balanced curriculum that “meets the needs of all pupils,” alongside our duty of care to keep our pupils safe. Our Preparing for Adulthood curriculum is tailored to the unique needs of our pupils, school, and school.
Preparing for Adulthood provides opportunities for pupils to learn about rights and responsibilities within society, build emotional literacy and resilience, and nurture their mental and physical health. Students will engage in a wide range of experiences and gain firsthand knowledge through meaningful activities both in the classroom and within the community. This includes opportunities to apply their skills in real-life settings, helping them to live healthy, safe, fulfilling, responsible, and balanced lives
Preparing for Adulthood is taught both as a standalone subject and integrated across other curriculum areas to ensure the knowledge and strategies are fully embedded in everyday learning.
At Fernways, we believe in giving back to our community. Our pupils take part in activities that bring people together, strengthen local links, and show them that they can make a positive difference. These experiences not only help pupils feel proud of their contributions but also build friendships, empathy and a sense of belonging.
Community Engagement highlights:
Our enrichment programme gives pupils the chance to discover new interests, celebrate their talents, and create lasting memories with their peers. These opportunities are central to helping our young people feel proud of who they are and confident in what they can achieve.
From lunchtime and after-school clubs such as Lego building, gardening and creative media, to specialist sessions including JAM Coding and STEM projects, pupils are encouraged to explore activities that spark curiosity and enjoyment. Sport and art are also central to our enrichment, giving pupils the chance to express themselves, develop teamwork, and build healthy habits.
We are proud of the many achievements that have come through enrichment at Fernways. Our student-led TV show, Good Morning Fernways, brings the school community together through news, interviews and creative features. Pupils have also reached national recognition through the Into Film Awards, where one student’s short documentary made it to the finals in London. Experiences like these show pupils that their voices and creativity matter — and can be celebrated well beyond the classroom.
Trips and wider opportunities also enrich school life. Pupils take part in cultural visits to theatres, galleries and museums, as well as life-skills trips where they practise travel training, shopping and engaging with the public in supportive environments. The Duke of Edinburgh Bronze Award adds another dimension, helping pupils to build resilience, teamwork and leadership in a structured and rewarding way.
Enrichment at Fernways is about creating joy, building friendships, and opening doors to experiences that pupils may never have tried before. These opportunities give our young people the chance to shine in different ways, to feel part of something bigger, and to leave school not just with qualifications, but with memories, achievements and passions that will stay with them for life.
Enrichment Highlights
At Fernways, our vocational offer is about much more than qualifications. It is designed to prepare pupils for life beyond school, giving them the skills, self-belief and independence they need to succeed in adulthood.
Our vocational curriculum supports wellbeing, develops employability, and builds the practical foundations for independence. Whether a pupil is moving on to college, an apprenticeship, or directly into the workplace, we ensure they leave Fernways ready to thrive.

These partnerships provide invaluable opportunities for pupils to apply their learning, build confidence and interact with employers and members of the public in safe, supported environments.
Practical Skills for Life
Through vocational learning, pupils gain a wide range of everyday skills that help them move towards independence. They learn to cook, garden, and carry out practical design work; build digital literacy; and develop teamwork and communication. They also practise managing money, shopping and using public transport. Each experience is carefully structured to reduce anxiety, increase independence, and prepare pupils for smoother transitions into further education, training or employment.
The Fernways Difference
Our vocational programme is not just about collecting certificates — it is about confidence for life. Pupils who once found new environments overwhelming learn to travel independently, manage money and engage with the wider community. Others discover new talents and interests that inspire their future pathways.
By the time they leave Fernways, pupils have not only gained qualifications but also the resilience, experiences and independence they need to step proudly into the wider world.
At Fernways, preparing our pupils for life beyond school is at the heart of everything we do. Careers education is woven into every stage of learning — from exploring strengths and interests in Year 7 to work experience, college visits and transition support in Year 11.
Our approach is guided by the Gatsby Benchmarks, adapted to meet the needs of autistic and SEN learners, and supported by our partnership with Innervate Careers Service. This ensures that every pupil receives high-quality, independent advice and practical experiences that prepare them for adulthood.

Choosing a school
Choosing the right specialist school for your child is a deeply personal and important decision. Every child is unique, and the right environment can make a world of difference in their development, happiness, and future.
Here's a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process:
1. Understand your child’s needs
Start by identifying your child’s specific educational, emotional and social needs. Consider:
Tip: Speak with your child’s current school, SENCO or healthcare professionals to build a clear picture.
Communication style and preferences
Learning strengths and challenges
Support needs (e.g. therapeutic input, behaviour support)
2. Know what specialist schools offer
Specialist schools vary widely. Look for:
Environment: Is it sensory-friendly, structured and nurturing?
3. Visit schools (in person or virtually)
A visit can reveal far more than a website. When visiting:
Ask: “How would you support a child like mine?”
Observe how staff interact with children
4. Ask the right questions
Here are some key questions to ask:
What therapies or interventions are available?
How do you celebrate progress and achievements?
5. Check reports and accreditation
Ofsted or equivalent inspection reports
Accreditation or specialist programmes (e.g. autism-friendly status)
Testimonials from other parents
6. Consider practicalities
Don’t forget the logistics:
Location and transport options
Class sizes and peer group dynamics
Funding and EHCP compatibility
Open days
See how learning comes to life in our schools.

Researched different types of specialist schools
Visited schools and asked key questions
Reviewed reports and parent feedback
Considered practicalities and funding
